newsitem.title: USA: Spain's Aznar confident on joining EMU on day one.
newsitem.headline: Spain's Aznar confident on joining EMU on day one.

text.p: Spanish Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar said on Thursday he was confident Spain would meet the economic targets required to join the European Monetary Union from the first day a single currency is launched.
Aznar added in a news conference that the EMU, slated to start on Jan. 1, 1999, would be completed on schedule since the initiative has already passed a point of no return.
"Investors in Wall Street naturally know that Spain is perfectly in condition to be part of the first group (of countries in the EMU) from day one," the conservative government leader said.

Aznar said Spain already meets the Maastricht treaty criteria on inflation, interest rates, currency stabilty, public sector deficit and public debt trends, arguing that his country was the least indebted nation in the European Union.
On the question of whether the EU will be able to launch the single currency on schedule, he said: "I believe we have already passed the point where you could turn back."

Aznar, here on the last day of a three-day trip to the United States, had talked to investors and bankers in New York on Tuesday and met with President Bill Clinton and several U.S. cabinet officials in Washington on Wednesday.
The Spanish government leader said that he and Clinton had agreed that bilateral relations were excellent, despite their differences over the U.S. legislation against Cuba.

Spain, along with its EU partners, objects strongly to the so-called Helms-Burton law, which prescribes sanctions for foreign companies that invest in properties confiscated from U.S. citizens and businesses in Cuba.
"There is not a single European country that will accept this law, now or ever, not because it concerns Cuba but... because of its extraterritorial provisions," Aznar said.

The EU last year challenged the validity of the U.S. law at the World Trade Organisation and only suspended its action after the White House agreed to try to negotiate a compromise solution to their disputes over foreign investments in rogue nations.
Under that understanding, the Clinton Administration would also seek authority from the United States Congress to waive sanctions under the Helms-Burton law against European companies.

Aznar said he could not predict whether Clinton would be able to deliver on those offers since the Democrats are in a minority in both houses of Congress, but recognised Washington's willingness to solve its disputes with its EU allies.
